lines: Every morning at six, Mr. Adisa walked to the roof of the meteorological office, read the rain gauge, and wrote the number in the ledger.
For thirty-one years the ledger did not once ask him how he was.
The week his wife left, it rained every day, and he wrote the numbers more carefully than ever, as though accuracy were a kind of prayer.
Nobody noticed that the handwriting had begun to shake.
On the ninth day a girl from the secretary pool climbed the stairs with two cups of tea.
She looked at the ledger, then at him, then at the sky.
"I mean today it's seventeen, and you've been writing it down as though it's yours."
He laughed for the first time in a month, a rusty, startled sound.
Then he took the pen, and in the margin, where the ledger kept its remarks, he wrote beside the number: Two cups of tea, shared.
